IIACSS · Iraq · 100 Days Survey · 2026

How Iraqis viewed al-Zaidi’s government after its first 100 days

The first 100 days offered an early view of how Iraqis assessed their new government and whether they believed its promises were translating into progress.

2,056 respondents August 5 to 31, 2026 ±3.5 percentage points
The first 100 days

What changed, and what did the findings suggest about the road ahead?

One hundred days represented a brief moment in the life of a country. For the new government, however, they provided an early test of whether promises had begun to translate into progress.

When Ali al-Zaidi was sworn in as Iraq’s prime minister on May 14, he arrived under unusual circumstances. A businessman with no previous government or political post, he was chosen as a consensus candidate after months of deadlock. He took office with an incomplete cabinet: parliament approved 14 ministers while nine ministries, including Interior and Defence, were still pending.

From his first day, the government faced overlapping pressures: oil exports, liquidity and public salaries, bringing weapons under state control, corruption, a deepening water and drought crisis, and a tense regional environment.

At the time of the survey, the government said it had opened files that had been delayed for years. It pointed to recovered public funds and gold, a new four-year government program, and reforms in finance and electricity. Critics argued that many of those decisions had not yet translated into tangible changes in daily life.

The central question was therefore not simply whether the government had acted, but whether Iraqis believed those actions were producing results.
01 · The opening mandate

Al-Zaidi began with a strong personal mandate.

The clearest finding was the prime minister’s relatively strong personal starting position. Seventy-seven percent said they were somewhat or fully satisfied with his selection, while 75 percent said he had borne the responsibilities of office to a great or moderate extent.

Those numbers did not establish whether the government had solved Iraq’s structural problems. Instead, they showed that, after a difficult formation process, al-Zaidi had begun with substantial public room to act. The charts documented that mandate from three angles: his selection, his overall evaluation, and whether Iraqis believed he had carried the weight of the office.

02 · Beyond the prime minister

Personal approval was not the same as confidence in the political system.

The new prime minister did not govern alone. The presidency, cabinet, parliament, its speaker, and the judiciary all shaped whether political decisions could be turned into durable policy.

That made the institutional ratings especially important. Read together, they indicated whether the early confidence surrounding al-Zaidi extended to the wider state, or whether the public distinguished between the prime minister and the institutions around him.

From individual officeholders to the institutions that supported the system.

The first three ratings focused on the president and the cabinet. The next group broadened the picture to Parliament, its speaker, and the judiciary, which shaped legislation, oversight, and the implementation of public decisions. Their evaluations helped identify where confidence in political leadership diverged from confidence in the institutions around it.

03 · From approval to delivery

The harder test was what people could feel in daily life.

The government said its first months had produced a 2026 to 2029 program, new financial coordination mechanisms, reforms in electricity, and a strategy to diversify oil export routes. The analysis assessed those announcements against perceptions of services, stability, and household experience.

The survey then moved from leadership to delivery. Iraqis were asked to judge the government on security, electricity, higher education, water, basic education, and health, areas where success or failure was experienced directly rather than through political messaging.

The resulting picture was uneven. Some areas received better ratings than others, supporting the interpretation of the first 100 days as an opening phase with mixed performance rather than a single verdict on the government.

Closer to daily life

The second half of the service assessment touched daily life more directly.

Security, electricity, and higher education revealed one side of state capacity. Water, basic education, and health brought the assessment directly into homes and communities. These were services people encountered repeatedly, so the analysis highlighted how slow improvement could narrow the political space created by a strong opening.

04 · The economic test

For many Iraqis, government performance was ultimately a household question.

Al-Zaidi inherited pressure around liquidity, public salaries, and an economy still heavily tied to oil. His government had pointed to financial reforms and efforts to diversify export routes, but the political value of those steps depended on whether citizens believed the broader economy was improving.

The survey captured both sides of that judgment: how Iraqis assessed the government’s economic performance up to that point, and what they expected over the following 12 months. Forty-six percent expected the economic situation to improve, a meaningful sign of optimism at the time, but not an unconditional vote of confidence.

05 · The corruption gap

Recovering funds and changing public perceptions were different tests.

The government said anti-corruption efforts had recovered $160 million, 380 billion Iraqi dinars, and 402 kilograms of gold. Those figures indicated claimed activity at the top of the state, but the harder question was whether Iraqis believed corruption itself was becoming less entrenched.

The survey showed the scale of the challenge. Sixty percent said corruption existed in state institutions and agencies to a great extent. That made anti-corruption performance a critical test of whether early government action could alter a much deeper public judgment.

06 · Expectations at the time

The government had political room to act.

The first 100 days did not settle the success or failure of the government. They revealed its starting position: relatively strong personal approval for the prime minister, more uneven confidence across institutions and services, cautious economic optimism, and a corruption problem that remained deeply embedded in public perception.

Seventy-one percent thought the al-Zaidi government would complete its constitutional four-year term. That finding suggested that many Iraqis expected continuity at the time of the survey. It did not establish confidence in future performance, and the analysis distinguished time in office from progress.

The first 100 days had given al-Zaidi a strong opening. The analysis identified the next test as the government’s ability to turn that political honeymoon into visible, durable results.

Conclusion

The first 100 days marked a starting point, rather than a final verdict.

The survey showed a government facing its next phase with an important advantage: many Iraqis were willing to give it time. Al-Zaidi's personal standing was stronger than confidence in several institutions, service delivery remained uneven, economic optimism was cautious, and corruption continued to shape how people judged the state.

The analysis identified both an opportunity and a clear standard. Early decisions would need to become improvements people could see in electricity, water, schools, health, the economy, and accountability for the first 100 days to provide a foundation for durable trust. It also suggested that early approval would be harder to sustain if those changes remained mostly at the level of announcements.

The opening mandate was clear. The analysis pointed to delivery as the measure of the next phase.
Source: Independent Institute for Administration and Civil Society Studies (IIACSS), published by the Atlantic Council in October 2026. Government achievement figures referenced in the article were reported as government claims.
